description_ru: Юмористический рассказ о поездке на свадьбу, в которой навигатор, пассажирка и собственная гордость водителя ведут неравную борьбу.
text:
I have never been a good driver, but until last summer I had always believed that I was an excellent navigator. This belief was based on a single occasion in 2009 when I found a petrol station without asking anyone, and it had sustained me through many years of confident wrong turns. It was my wife, Celia, who finally persuaded me to use a satnav, and she did so on the morning of her cousin's wedding, in a tone that suggested the matter was no longer open to discussion.

The wedding was in a village called Little Wickham, a place that, according to the invitation, was "easy to find". I have noticed that people who describe a place as easy to find are always the sort of people who have lived there all their lives. The invitation included a hand-drawn map with a church, a duck pond and an arrow labelled "you". I considered this adequate. Celia considered it a work of fiction, and plugged the satnav into the dashboard with a brisk click.

The device spoke in the voice of a calm woman who sounded as though she taught yoga. "In four hundred metres," she said, "turn left." I did not turn left, because the road had a perfectly good continuation straight ahead, and because I did not enjoy being told. "Recalculating," she said, in a tone of such gentle disappointment that I felt as though I had forgotten a birthday. Celia looked out of the window and said nothing, which is her way of saying a great deal.

For the first hour, we conducted what I would describe as a negotiation. The satnav proposed a route, and I proposed a better one, which was generally the same route with a more interesting history. "Take the next exit," she said. "I know a shortcut," I said, and took a road that I vaguely remembered from a cycling holiday in 1998. It ended, a little unexpectedly, in a farmyard. A farmer in a flat cap looked at us with the patient expression of a man who sees several of us every summer, and pointed silently in the direction from which we had come.

"Make a U-turn when possible," said the satnav, and the way she said "possible" implied that she had her doubts. By then Celia had begun to read the map on her phone aloud, in the weary voice of a hostage who knows that no help is coming. I reminded her that the satnav had also taken us, a few weeks earlier, on a route which included a ford, but she remarked that the ford had been my idea, and that the satnav had, in fact, advised against it.

The second hour passed in a kind of grim harmony. I had decided, perhaps out of fatigue, to obey the satnav entirely, and I was surprised to discover that it was strangely restful. It is a peculiar relief to give up responsibility. I turned where she told me to turn, I went straight where she told me to go straight, and I became, for a short while, an instrument of the machine, a sort of well-dressed robot with a steering wheel. We passed fields, a windmill and a sign for a village called Nether Snoring, which Celia photographed with the first smile of the afternoon.

It was at this moment of fragile peace that we came to a roundabout. "At the roundabout," said the satnav, "take the third exit." I counted. There were four exits, which was fine, but one of them was blocked by a tractor, which was less fine, and I could not decide whether the tractor counted. I went round once and then, in the interest of thoroughness, a second time. On the third circuit, I noticed that a small crowd of cyclists had gathered at the side of the road and was watching me with open interest. One of them raised a thermos in salute.

"Perhaps," Celia said, in the careful voice of a diplomat, "we could try the other exit." I took the exit that the satnav had not mentioned, partly out of spite and partly because I was dizzy. The satnav said, with infinite tenderness, "Recalculating," and then, after a short pause, "You have arrived at your destination." This was impressive, as the destination was a field.

We got out of the car. The field contained fourteen cows, a gate and a very small stream. There was no church, no duck pond, and no arrow labelled "you". Celia stood for a long moment with her hands on her hips and her face composed in the expression of someone choosing which of three insults to deploy first. I remember the cows watching us with a kind of detached sympathy.

In the end, it was the farmer who saved us. A different farmer, naturally, although he, too, wore a flat cap, and he gave us directions in the clear, unhurried language of a man who knows his own land. "Little Wickham?" he said. "You want the other Little Wickham. This one is Little Wickham Magna. Everyone gets it wrong." I asked why nobody had mentioned that, and he looked at me with a mild pity. "It's on the signpost," he said.

We reached the wedding forty minutes late and slipped into the back of the church just as the bride was coming down the aisle, with the enormous relief of two people who have been through something together. After the ceremony, Celia's cousin asked how our journey had been. "Wonderful," said Celia, with perfect composure. "Very scenic. Matthew was in charge of the navigation."

On the way home I was silent, and the satnav was silent too, perhaps from tact. As we turned into our own street, a familiar voice said, quietly, "You have arrived." I took this as an olive branch. It was the first time all day that she and I had agreed on anything, and I thanked her. Celia, in the passenger seat, put her hand over her mouth, and I realised that she was laughing so hard she could not speak.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка поднят и не касается нёба, без раскатистости: road, route.
Губы вытянуты вперёд и раскрываются: wedding, wife. Не заменяйте на в.
Долгий звук, губы расслаблены: turn, word.
NAvigator, negoTiation, destiNAtion: в -ation ударение падает на слог перед суффиксом, а в navigator на первый.

questions.question: Why was the couple driving to Little Wickham?
What did the satnav say when the writer ignored it?
Where did the satnav finally take them?
Why was it the wrong place?
questions.answer: There were two villages; they needed the other Little Wickham.
